open-question.question: Which plugin copy does the agy suite drive — the copy already installed at ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn as it stands, the freshly built hosts/antigravity/ tree that the suite installs over that path before running, or a copy installed under an isolated HOME the suite sets for the agy process so the user's own installation is never touched?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: Every run is guaranteed to test the current build at the real global path with the user's real credentials while writing nothing to the user's installation; the isolated-HOME and symlink forms rest on unverified host behaviour, the overwrite forms replace the user's install with a development tree, and the one extra copy step costs a command the stop line names.
open-question.alternative: Source: the copy already at ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn. Location: the user's real HOME. Install step: none, but before any agy process starts the suite compares that copy byte for byte with the repository's hosts/antigravity/ tree and stops on any difference, naming the remedy (re-extract or copy the built tree). It writes nothing to the user's installation. Every run is guaranteed to test the current build while the suite still never writes to the user's installation. Replacing the copy stays an explicit act of the user's own, and a stale install is caught rather than silently tested. Every build change makes the developer copy the tree by hand before the suite will run, which turns a one-command check into two steps. The comparison has to define which files count (the tree's README, .github workflow, and LICENSE ship too). How the suite reports a missing copy, as opposed to a different one, belongs to the sibling question on running without agy.

Source: the copy already at ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn, whatever release or build it holds. Location: the user's real HOME. Install step: none. The suite installs, compares, and restores nothing. It drives agy against that path and leaves keeping the copy current to the person running it. It is the simplest suite and never writes outside its fixture workspace. It exercises exactly the installation a user has, the same path the kinga_page failure ran against, and it can never disturb the user's own setup. A pass or fail says nothing about the change under test unless the user remembered to re-extract the freshly built tree first. Today the copy is a byte-identical 1.8.5 tree carrying the old .agents/plugins/cairn literal and no enable_write_tools key, so a run made after the milestone's build changes, with no reinstall, would test the old tree and report its old failures, or a stale pass.

Source: the freshly built hosts/antigravity/ tree. Location: the user's real HOME. Install step: before running, the suite replaces ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn with a copy of the built tree and leaves it there afterwards, with no backup or restore. One command always tests the current build, at the exact global path the milestone standardizes on, with the user's real agy credentials, trusted folders, and git identity. The resulting install is also the next release's tree, so the maintainer's own agy setup tracks the build. The suite silently overwrites the user's own installation with an unreleased build. Every other project the user runs agy in (kinga_page, for one) then loads that development tree until the user re-extracts a release, and a running agy session picks it up only on restart. A run on a contributor's machine replaces their installed release without asking.

Source: the freshly built hosts/antigravity/ tree. Location: the user's real HOME. Install step: the suite moves any existing ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn aside, copies the built tree into that path, runs, and on exit (pass, fail, or interrupt) removes its copy and moves the user's original back. If no copy stood there before, it leaves none behind. It tests the current build at the real global path with the user's real credentials and environment, and it leaves the user's installation as it found it once the run ends. While the suite runs, every agy session on the machine sees the development tree. A crash or kill between the move and the restore can strand the original under a backup name and leave the development tree installed. The suite also needs delete and move logic over a directory inside the user's own configuration, which is the riskiest code it would carry.

Source: the repository's hosts/antigravity/ tree itself, not a copy. Location: the user's real HOME. Install step: ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn is made a symbolic link to the checkout's hosts/antigravity/ (once by the developer, or by the suite whenever the path is not already that link) and stays in place, so every rebuild is live at the global path with no install step per run. The suite always drives the current build, and no copying happens on any run. The maintainer's agy picks up each rebuild the way their Claude Code setup already loads hosts/claude live. Whether agy resolves the link and reports the skill's absolute SKILL.md path as the repository location rather than ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn has not been verified. A suite meant to prove global plugin-root resolution could therefore pass against a path no user install ever has. Every agy session on the machine also loads uncommitted development state, and a user who installs releases is left with a link instead.

Source: the freshly built hosts/antigravity/ tree. Location: a temporary directory the suite creates and sets as HOME for each agy process. Install step: the suite copies the built tree to that directory's .gemini/config/plugins/cairn, and copies in the minimum agy needs to run (the OAuth credentials and account files under ~/.gemini, plus a git identity for the fixture's commits). It never writes to the user's real ~/.gemini. Every run tests the current build at the global path's real shape, relative to the HOME the process sees, and it never touches the user's installation or any running agy session. Leftover state from an earlier run or a stale workspace-local copy cannot leak in. Whether agy 1.4.0 derives its config root from HOME, and authenticates from copied oauth_creds.json alone without a keychain or a fresh login, is unverified. The suite would also copy live OAuth credentials into a temp directory. Changing HOME changes git config, uv caches, and anything else the run reads from it. Whether the tree's plugin-root literal resolves inside the isolated HOME depends on the sibling question on the plugin-root literal form.

open-question.question: Which surfaces does the suite's plugin-root resolution test cover — the orchestrator's file read of a shared procedure, its python3 tool command, and the same two inside a dispatched agent, or only the tool command — given that the report's failures showed up on both the file read and the command?
open-question.recommendation: Pins both failure modes the report observed in one dispatch-free process whose printed output asserts the read and the command separately, while the agent context's reads and commands are exercised by the subagent probe's real-input dispatches, whose landed files cannot appear without them; asserting an agent's read on its own would need a foreign prompt or an undocumented transcript format.
open-question.alternative: The resolution test covers the orchestrator only, on both surfaces: its file read of a shared procedure and its python3 tool command; no dispatched agent's resolution is asserted by this test. It pins both failure modes the report observed in the orchestrator — the view_file stat failure and python's exit 2 — in one headless agy process with no dispatch, keeping the test fast and its pass signal simple. The dispatched agent, whose prompt carries no plugin path and which never sees the absolute SKILL.md path the orchestrator receives, is exactly where a form that relies on that metadata would fail, and this test does not look there; agent-side resolution is then verified only if the subagent probe happens to exercise it, which depends on the shape that probe takes.

The resolution test covers all four surfaces in both rendered agents: the orchestrator's file read of a shared procedure and its python3 tool command, and inside each dispatched agent (provide-alternatives-to-open-question and complete-task) its own file read of a shared procedure (alternatives-procedure.md, complete-procedure.md) and its own tool command (open_questions.py, task_list.py), each surface asserted separately. Every place the report saw a path fail is pinned, and each agent's distinct procedure file and tool is exercised, so a literal form that resolves in the shell but not in the host's file-reading tool, or in the orchestrator but not in an agent whose prompt carries no plugin path, fails a named assertion rather than a later run. It is the costliest shape: at least two agent dispatches per run, each a slow headless agy process using model calls, and complete-task needs a fixture task it can complete; how cheaply the agent surfaces can be reached depends on the shape the subagent probe takes and the fixture workspace the suite uses.

The resolution test covers all four surfaces — the orchestrator's file read of a shared procedure and its python3 tool command, and the same two inside one dispatched agent (provide-alternatives-to-open-question, the agent the report observed failing) — and does not dispatch complete-task for resolution. Both failure surfaces are covered in both contexts the report distinguishes, including the agent whose prompt carries no plugin path, at the cost of a single agent dispatch; both agents' rendered literals come from the same plugin_root, so one agent stands in for the other's resolution. complete-task's own read of complete-procedure.md and its task_list.py command go unexercised, so a fault specific to that agent file's rendering or context is caught only by its write-tools probe, if that probe touches those paths; whether it does depends on the shape the subagent probe takes.

The resolution test covers the python3 tool command only, in both contexts: once run by the orchestrator and once run inside a dispatched agent; no file read of a shared procedure is asserted in either. A failed command is loud and mechanically checkable (a non-zero exit and a no-such-file line in the transcript or output), whereas a failed file read may be silently recovered by the model searching for the file, so the test keys on the unambiguous signal while still covering the agent context the orchestrator's metadata does not reach. The host's file-reading tool and the shell resolve paths differently (the shell expands a tilde or $HOME, a file-reading tool may not), so a literal form that passes the command check can still break every shared-procedure read; whether that gap matters depends on the literal form chosen for the plugin root.

The resolution test covers one surface in one context: the orchestrator's python3 tool command; neither file reads nor any dispatched agent is asserted. It is the smallest, fastest, and least flaky test: one headless agy process, no dispatch, and a pass signal (the tool's output or exit status) that needs no transcript inspection. It covers one of the four places the report's failures appeared, leaving the file-read surface and the agent context — the two places a literal form is most likely to resolve differently — to be caught only by a later real run; how much that leaves exposed depends on the literal form chosen for the plugin root.

The suite carries no separate resolution test: plugin-root resolution is treated as verified whenever the end-to-end subagent check passes, since that run cannot succeed unless the orchestrator's and the agent's reads and commands resolved; no surface is asserted on its own. It adds no extra agy process or assertion beyond what the suite already runs, keeping the on-demand suite as short and cheap as possible while still failing when resolution is broken. A failure reports only that the run failed, not which surface or context broke, and a model that recovers from a failed read by searching for the file can pass with a broken literal; whether the end-to-end check touches any given surface at all depends on the shape the subagent probe takes.

open-question.question: In what workspace does the agy suite run each headless agy process — a temporary git repository the suite seeds through the plugin's own tools with a milestone and open questions, a committed fixture directory under tests/fixtures/ copied to a temporary location, or the cairn repository checkout itself?
open-question.recommendation: A static, reviewable starting state in the copy-to-temp pattern the suite already uses, holding the bare questions and the one trivial task the direct dispatches need, so setup depends on no plugin tool being correct and a failure points at the host integration; a fixture gone stale is caught by the tools refusing it at run time.
open-question.alternative: A new committed directory under tests/fixtures/ holds a small project tree (milestones/README.md with its pointer, one milestone directory with requirements.md, open_questions.xml holding a few bare blocks, and the two task files); for each agy process the suite copies it to a fresh temporary directory, as conftest.py's milestone_dir fixture already does for the tool tests, then runs git init and an initial commit there, since a nested .git cannot be committed inside the fixture. The starting state is static, reviewable in a diff, and identical on every run, following the copy-to-tmp_path pattern the suite already uses, so the setup depends on no plugin tool being correct and a failure points at the host integration. The fixture is a second hand-maintained copy of the milestone layout: a later change to the file set or the XML form leaves it stale with nothing checking it, and the git initialisation still has to be scripted per run.

Each agy process runs in its own fresh git repository under the system temp location (a pytest tmp_path or a mktemp -d directory), which the suite builds at run time: git init, a milestones/README.md with its Current milestone: pointer written by the suite itself (no tool writes that file), the milestone directory created by define_milestone.py from a goal piped on stdin, its open questions appended by open_questions.py add, and an initial commit, all before the agy -p line runs with that directory as its working directory. The workspace is always in the exact layout and canonical XML form the current tools produce, so it can never drift from the milestone format the plugin expects, and every run starts from a clean, isolated, reproducible state that no earlier run or the cairn history can disturb. The seed is code to maintain: the question texts and goal live as strings in the suite, the README pointer is still hand-written, and a bug in define_milestone.py or open_questions.py breaks the agy suite's setup rather than surfacing as an Antigravity finding, which blurs what a failure means.

Each agy process runs with the cairn repository checkout itself as its working directory, against whatever milestone milestones/README.md currently points at, with no workspace created, copied, or seeded by the suite. No setup at all: the workspace is a real cairn-managed project with real milestones, so the run is as close to a user's use as the repository can offer. The runs write into the maintainer's own history: a committing skill lands Alternatives-annotation or other commits on the current milestone, the result depends on that milestone's live state (or fails outright when the pointer reads none), runs are not reproducible or isolable, and the checkout's own AGENTS.md and dirty working tree can steer or block the agent.

Each agy process runs in its own fresh, empty git repository under the system temp location, holding no milestones/ directory, pointer, or open questions; whatever a test needs (a file to write, a command to run) is named in its prompt rather than pre-seeded. The smallest possible workspace, with nothing to seed or maintain and no dependence on the milestone format, so the suite checks only plugin-root resolution and subagent tool execution and nothing else can fail it. It is viable only if the sibling questions on the subagent probe's shape and the resolution test's surfaces settle on probes that need no milestone; a full cairn skill run, or a python3 tool command over a milestone directory, has nothing to operate on here.

open-question.question: When the agy suite is invoked on a machine where agy is not on PATH or the global plugin copy it needs is absent, does it skip its tests, fail them, or stop before any test with one line naming the missing prerequisite?
open-question.recommendation: A requested verification must never read green on a machine that verified nothing; a session-level stop naming the missing agy, the missing global copy, or an installed copy that differs from the build is harmless because the suite's own directory keeps it out of every default run, and one line names the cause where per-test failures would bury it.
open-question.alternative: Before any test runs, the suite checks both prerequisites (agy resolvable on PATH, the global plugin copy present at ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn) in one up-front check. When either is missing, it stops the whole run with a non-zero exit and one line naming the missing prerequisite. It reports no per-test outcome, and it treats both prerequisites the same way. An explicitly requested verification can never come back green on a machine that verified nothing. The single line names the exact cause, and no agy process is started only to fail, which keeps the report readable for the contributor or release pre-flight that asked for the run. Aborting the run is only harmless if the suite is never collected as part of a broader run. If it lives somewhere a wholesale pytest invocation reaches it (the Suite location and invocation axis), a session-level stop on a machine without agy breaks that unrelated run instead of passing it by. It also needs a session-level hook or a separate entry point rather than the ordinary per-test idiom.

Every suite test is skipped with a reason naming the missing prerequisite, and the run exits 0. This is a module-level skip in the manner of tests/test_build_rendering.py, which skips itself below Python 3.11 keyed on a condition checked before anything else, or one equivalent message and a zero exit if the suite is not pytest. Both prerequisites are treated the same way. It follows the repository's one existing conditional-module convention and the standard pytest idiom. That makes it harmless wherever the suite is collected on a machine without agy, CI's ubuntu job included, so the default run stays unchanged whatever the suite's location turns out to be. A run someone asked for on a misconfigured machine exits 0 with everything skipped, and the exit code reads as success. A contributor gate or release pre-flight that keys on the result can then pass without exercising agy at all, which defeats the point of a suite that runs only when someone wants the integration verified.

The suite is collected and run as normal, and each test (through a shared fixture or per-test guard) fails with a message naming the missing prerequisite. The run exits non-zero and reports one failure per test, and both prerequisites are treated the same way. It stays within ordinary per-test pytest machinery, needing no session-level abort hook, while still guaranteeing that a requested run on an unprepared machine cannot read as a pass. The report shows as many identical failures as the suite has tests, which buries the single real cause. It shares the stop option's hazard of turning any broader collection on a machine without agy red (the Suite location and invocation axis), with noisier output.

The two prerequisites are treated differently. When agy is not on PATH, every test is skipped with a reason naming agy and the run exits 0, because the machine simply cannot run the suite. When agy is present but the global plugin copy is absent, the run fails non-zero with a line naming the missing copy, because the installation this milestone standardizes on is missing on a machine set up for agy. The outcome follows what the absence means. A machine without the host is not a finding, while a host without the global install is exactly the kind of setup fault the global-path standardization is meant to rule out, so it is reported loudly. The split only makes sense if the suite drives the pre-installed global copy. If it installs its own copy, the second prerequisite never arises (the Suite plugin copy axis). It also keeps the skip option's risk that a requested run on a machine without agy exits 0, and it is two rules to document instead of one.

The suite skips with a reason naming the missing prerequisite and exits 0 by default. An explicit switch the suite documents (an environment variable or command-line flag) turns the same missing prerequisite into a stop before any test, with a non-zero exit and one line naming it. Both prerequisites get the same treatment in each mode. Any accidental or wholesale collection stays harmless, and a deliberate verification (a contributor gate or release pre-flight) can still demand that a missing prerequisite fail instead of passing silently. It adds a second mode and a switch that every invoking site must remember to set. A gate that forgets the flag silently falls back to the skip behaviour and its false green. It is also more mechanism than a suite that already runs only on request may need.

The suite adds no detection of either prerequisite. Its tests invoke agy and read the global copy directly, and on a machine lacking either they fail with whatever the subprocess or agy itself raises: a FileNotFoundError for a missing binary, or agy's own error or a failed resolution for a missing copy. It adds no code and leaves no prerequisite list to keep in step with what the tests actually use. Any missing piece still makes the run non-zero. The failure names no prerequisite. A missing global copy surfaces as a plugin-root resolution failure that looks exactly like the bug the suite exists to detect, so an unprepared machine produces a misleading regression report rather than a setup message.

open-question.question: How is the goal's rule that the agy suite runs when the Antigravity host integration changes realized, with CI ruled out — a CONTRIBUTING.md sentence naming the paths whose change requires a run before committing, a pre-flight step in the release-plugin skill, or both?
open-question.recommendation: A run is expected at commit time, where a failure is cheapest to fix, and enforced at release time, the one point a broken Antigravity tree reaches users, while Claude- or Codex-only releases pay nothing; the gate stays within the pre-flight's no-write rule because the suite writes nothing to the installation, and a shared four-item path set is cheap to keep in step.
open-question.alternative: Both mechanisms over one shared narrow path set (scripts/hosts/antigravity/, core/agents/*.md, scripts/build_hosts.py, the suite). A CONTRIBUTING.md ## Development sentence requires a run before committing a change to those paths. A release-plugin pre-flight check runs the suite when those paths changed since the last tag and stops the release on a failure. A run is expected at commit time, when a failure is cheapest to fix, and enforced at release time, when it would otherwise reach users. So a skipped commit-time run is still caught before publication. The path list lives in two files that must be kept in step by hand. A commit-time run that was skipped is caught only at release. It inherits the release gate's conditions on the sibling suite-without-agy and plugin-copy questions.

A sentence in CONTRIBUTING.md's ## Development section, beside the two pytest runs and the rule that both must pass before a tool change is committed. It names a narrow path set whose change requires an agy suite run before committing: the Antigravity definition directory scripts/hosts/antigravity/ (plugin_root, strip_frontmatter_keys, slots, templates), the agent sources core/agents/*.md, scripts/build_hosts.py, and the suite itself. The release-plugin skill is not changed and nothing enforces the rule. It is one sentence in the file that already holds every test-run rule. It fires only on the files that produced this milestone's two failures (the plugin-root literal and the agent frontmatter), so a run costs real agy time and model calls only when the integration itself moved. It is advisory. Nothing stops a commit or a release that skipped the run. A core/ change that breaks Antigravity some other way, such as a new shared-procedure path or a new python3 command form in a skill, falls outside the list and is never checked. The command it names depends on how the sibling suite-location question settles.

The same CONTRIBUTING.md ## Development sentence, but its trigger is broad: any commit that changes a file under hosts/antigravity/. Since that tree is rebuilt and committed with every core/ change, this means nearly every runtime change. The release-plugin skill is not changed and nothing enforces the rule. The trigger matches the rendered artifact Antigravity actually loads, so no breaking change can fall outside it. It is also checkable at a glance with git diff --stat, with no path list to maintain as the integration's sources move. Nearly every commit would need a slow, model-backed agy run, which makes the rule costly enough to be skipped routinely. That erodes what it is meant to guarantee, and it is still advisory with nothing to catch a skipped run.

A new pre-flight check in .claude/skills/release-plugin/SKILL.md step 2. It runs git diff --name-only between the last release tag and HEAD over the narrow path set (scripts/hosts/antigravity/, core/agents/*.md, scripts/build_hosts.py, the suite). When any of those changed, it runs the agy suite and stops the release on a failure. No CONTRIBUTING.md sentence is added. It is enforced at the one point where a broken Antigravity tree reaches users, the publish into cairn-antigravity. It reuses the last-tag value step 1 already resolves, and releases with no integration change pay nothing. A regression is caught only at release, possibly many commits after it landed, when it is harder to bisect. The skill never waives a gate, so a release cut on a machine without agy is blocked outright unless the gate handles that case, which depends on the sibling suite-without-agy question. If the suite installs over the global copy (the sibling plugin-copy question), the step breaks the pre-flight's rule that no check writes anything.

A new pre-flight check in the release-plugin skill's step 2 that runs the agy suite on every release, whatever changed, and stops the release on a failure. No path list exists and no CONTRIBUTING.md sentence is added. It is the simplest enforced form. There is no path list to keep current and no way for an unlisted file to slip past, so every published Antigravity tree has passed the real agy CLI. Every release, including Claude- or Codex-only patch releases, pays the suite's time and model cost and needs agy installed. Like the conditional gate, it catches a regression only at release, and it carries the same conditions on the sibling suite-without-agy and plugin-copy questions.

A CONTRIBUTING.md ## Development sentence that names the narrow path set for commit-time runs, together with a release-plugin pre-flight check that runs the agy suite on every release, whatever changed, and stops the release on a failure. The commit-time list stays short and cheap to follow, while the unconditional release run backs it up for anything the list misses, such as a core/ change that breaks Antigravity outside the named paths. No path list has to be duplicated in the release skill. It has the highest standing cost: every release needs agy and pays a suite run even when nothing Antigravity-related changed, and contributors still have the advisory sentence to follow. It carries the same sibling conditions as the other release-gate options.

The trigger rule, with the narrow path set, is written as a point under CLAUDE.md's ## Development section instead of CONTRIBUTING.md, so that every agent session working in the repository, including complete-task agents executing milestone tasks, loads it. The release-plugin skill is not changed. Most changes here are made by agents running milestone tasks, and CLAUDE.md is the one file every such session loads automatically. So the rule reaches the runner most likely to make an integration change and able to run the suite as part of its acceptance bar. CLAUDE.md states that the build loop and test runs are documented in CONTRIBUTING.md, with CLAUDE.md holding only points not recorded there. Putting a test-run rule there splits that home, and human contributors reading CONTRIBUTING.md never see it. It is still advisory, with nothing at release to catch a skipped run.

No sentence, gate, or context line is added. The suite runs only when the maintainer chooses to run it, and the goal's "when the Antigravity host integration changes" is left to the maintainer's judgment for good rather than written down anywhere. It adds no prose, no path list to maintain, and no release dependency on agy. It fits a single-maintainer project where the person changing the Antigravity integration is the same person who wrote the suite. The goal names the integration-change trigger as part of what the milestone delivers, so leaving it unrealized arguably leaves the goal half met. Nothing records when a run is due, so the next plugin-root or frontmatter regression can ship exactly as this milestone's two failures did.

open-question.question: What becomes of the dated hands-on-check block in the header of scripts/hosts/antigravity/settings.toml once a repeatable suite exists — this milestone's run updates it to name agy 1.4.0, the global path, and the write-tools check and it stays the one record of what was checked, or it is replaced by a pointer to the suite as the way to re-check?

This milestone's run rewrites the dated block as a new check against agy 1.4.0, naming the global path, the enable_write_tools check, and the carried or re-checked slot-sourcing points, and the block stays the one record of what was checked. A dated block that says what was checked on its date stays true as history, and the suite carries the new checks without any decision about how the two records relate. Goes against the invariant's own rule that a later re-check updates the block: this milestone's run is such a re-check, against a newer agy and a different install path, and it would leave no committed trace. The block would keep describing a workspace-relative install the milestone makes unsupported, misleading the next editor about which version and which layout the slot values were last confirmed against.
